
Assignment Type: Annotated bibliography
Mode of Organization: Annotated bibliography with a one-paragraph description 
of each entry
Length: 600–800 words
Research Requirements: Extensive. You are required to use the AU Library.
Weight: 10% of your final grade
You will determine if the sources are reliable and relevant, select information from
those sources, and create an annotated bibliography.
An annotated bibliography is a tool. It helps you familiarize yourself with available
sources. It helps you keep track of the various sources you have consulted. It gives 
you a quick overview of what each source contributes to your topic. It helps to 
show connections between sources. It makes your research transparent, which 
helps validate the research. Finally, it can offer an outline of the various theories, 
arguments, interpretations, issues, research, and evidence in a particular field or 
about a particular topic.

For Assignment 5, you will write one essay—a classification essay or a 
comparison essay or a cause-and effect essay—based on one of the topics below.
You will use this topic for both Assignment 4 (in which you create an annotated 
bibliography) and
Assignment 5 (in which you write the complete 
essay).

Comparison Essay
Choose one of the topics below. To write a well-structured, well-researched 
comparison essay, work through the Learning Activities in Units 4 and 5 and refer 
to Chapter 16 of Read, Think, Write. Remember, you will need to narrow the topic,
and you must establish a purpose for making the comparison. To support the thesis,
use a point-by-point comparison structure in the body of the essay.
1. Compare two high-profile professional actors, singers, comedians, or 
athletes.
2. Compare a particular aspect of two Indigenous cultures in Canada.
3. Compare Kindergarten – Grade 12 education in Canada and another country.
4. In consultation with your tutor, you may develop your own topic for this 
essay. Do not proceed with your own topic until you have consulted your tutor.

Cause-and-Effect Essay
Choose one of the topics below. To write a well-structured, well-researched cause-
and-effect essay, work through the Learning Activities in Units 4 and 5 and refer to
Chapter 16 of Read, Think, Write. You will need to narrow the topic and develop a 
thesis. To support the thesis, you may choose to write about only causes, only 
effects, or causes and effects. Choose one of the essay structures provided in 
Chapter 16.
5. Examine the effects of wildfires in Canada.
6. Examine the causes or effects of microplastics in the ocean.
7. Examine the cause and/or effects of the digital divide.
8. In consultation with your tutor, you may develop your own topic for this 
essay. Do not proceed with your own topic until you have consulted your tutor.

Classification Essay
Choose one of the topics below. To write a well-structured, well-researched 
classification essay, work through the Learning Activities in Units 4 and 5 and 
refer to Chapter 16 of Read, Think, Write. Remember, you will need to narrow the 
topic, and you must establish a purpose for the classification.
9. Choose one genre of music (such as jazz, blues, rap, country, rock, classical, pop, or other). Classify and describe two to three well-recognized sub-genres of this style of music.
10.Choose one genre of film (such as thriller, romantic comedy, fantasy, science fiction, spoof, space movie, or other). Classify and describe two to three well-recognized sub-genres of this type of film.
11.Classify the types of one of the following as they are portrayed in a particular medium: wizards, vampires, or zombies.
12.In consultation with your tutor, you may develop your own topic for this essay. Do not proceed with your own topic until you have consulted your tutor.

Checklist for Assignment 4
After you have completed all of the required readings and followed all steps in 
Unit 4 to create your annotated bibliography, use the checklist below to evaluate 
whether it is ready for submission. If necessary, revise it before submitting it for 
marking.
•	Is the annotated bibliography formatted according to the assignment format guidelines of MLA or APA style? (Refer to LA 10.) Are margins, indentation, and spacing correct? 
•	Did you compare the formatting of your assignment to the sample annotated bibliography on the Purdue OWL?
•	Have you used APA style or MLA style consistently throughout the assignment?
•	Does the bibliography contain five or six sources relevant to the topic for the Assignment 5 essay?
•	Are at least three of the sources from peer-reviewed scholarly journals?
•	Does each section begin with a correctly formatted bibliography entry?
•	Are the sections arranged in alphabetical order, according to the authors’ last names?
•	Does each section contain a paragraph of approximately 100 words?
•	Does each paragraph briefly summarize the article, comment on the reliability of the source, and reflect on the relevance to your Assignment 5 essay?
•	Is every research source reputable and reliable?
•	Have the paragraphs been edited for style?
•	Are grammar and mechanics correct?
•	Did you get your articles froms the Athabasca Library?

Learn about the documentation of research sources
Carefully read the following chapters in Read, Think, Write so that you 
understand how to choose appropriate research sources, what documentation 
is, and why documenting sources is so important in academic writing. Pay 
careful attention to what constitutes plagiarism.

•	Chapter 20: Research Sources: Finding and Selecting Relevant, Reliable Sources
•	Chapter 22: Documentation: Plagiarism, Citations, and the List of Sources

Learn about MLA-style or APA-style bibliographical referencing
In Units 1 and 3, you chose a documentation format that is best for your area 
of study. Now, we encourage you to become even better acquainted with the 
intricacies of bibliographical referencing in your chosen style. In MLA style, 
the list of sources is titled “Works Cited.” In APA style, the list of sources is 
called “References.”
Whichever style you choose, we recommend the Purdue Online Writing Lab 
for all documentation matters:
•	If you are using MLA style, visit Purdue OWL’s MLA Formatting and Style  Guide page and study it carefully. Note that in the left column, you will find a link to basic format guidelines that apply to all sources on the Works Cited list. You will also find links to instructions for formatting entries for specific types of sources, such as a book, an article in a periodical (journal, newspaper, magazine), a website, and others.
•	If you are using APA style, visit Purdue OWL’s APA Formatting and Style Guide page and study it carefully. Note that in the left column, you will find a link to basic format guidelines that apply to all sources on the References List. You will also find links to instructions for formatting entries for specific types of sources, such as a book, an article in a periodical (journal, newspaper, magazine), electronic sources (such as websites), and others.
You may also want to refer to the AU’s Write Site’s excellent resource The 
Basics of Documentation , which is in a printable PDF format.

e. Locate and record the following bibliographic information for James Hutson's article:
•	Title of the article
•	Name of the author
•	Title of the journal that published the article
•	Volume and issue number
•	Date of publication
•	Page number(s)—if the page numbers are not listed in the article description, open a DF of the article to see the original text, on which the page numbers will be printed
•	Link—the preferred link includes a digital object identifier (doi) number, which always begins with the number 10. Sometimes the doi is located inside a URL; other times, it is recorded like this: doi: 10.3990/soc12040102
•	Database Title—database titles are required for MLA Works Cited lists—find this information in the description of the article from the library search page

Follow this link to learn how to locate the bibliographic information you'll need: https://athabascau.libanswers.com/faq/211539 
The first example is for a book titled Halfbreed. All the bibliographic  information you need is presented directly below the title. An arrow on the right points to a permalink, which is a link you'll need to include in your essay's bibliography. There is an arrow pointing to “Add to folder.” Please ignore this because we suggest avoiding the folders feature. Instead, save PDFs to your computer.
Now, scroll down to see a second example, for an article titled "Water Security in Indigenous Canada: A Community-Based Interdisciplinary Approach." Immediately below the article title is the information you need for your bibliography: the authors' names, the title of the journal, the volume number, the issue number, the publication date, the page range, and the doi number (which is a permanent, or persistent, link). Below that, you would click on “Full text – PDF,” which you would open and save to your computer.
In both samples, you'll also see an arrow pointing to a “Cite” button in the top right corner. Ignore that because the citation will be unreliable. When you are constructing your bibliography, do not use the URL in the browser address bar. (That URL is search-specific, so it will not open for your instructor.) To locate the correct link, click the "Permalink" button. The pop-up box contains the URL that you will copy and paste into the entry on your bibliography.

g. Check your entry against the information here, and pay particular attention to spacing, capitalization, punctuation, and italicization.
Don't trust the prepared bibliography entries on articles or the fill-in-the-blank templates for creating bibliography entries, which are available as templates in Microsoft Word, on Purdue OWL (in the box that says “cite your source automatically”), and elsewhere. Don’t use them! Don't trust the “Cite This Source” button that materializes in a library search. It important that you learn to create the bibliography yourself, following the formatting guidelines of MLA or APA style. Create each bibliography entry on your own, without the use of a template.

Choose a topic for Assignment 5
h. When you have received your list of topics for Assignment 5 from your tutor, browse the list and identify a few topics that you think you might like to write an essay on.
i. Circle three topics that seem most interesting to you. The topics are likely to be fairly broad, so take a moment to consider what specific aspect of the topic is of interest.
j. Give yourself at least a few hours before going back to the list and selecting one topic to proceed with.
Narrow the topic
The topics on the Assignment 5 Topic List are too broad (big) to manage in a  four-page essay. You would need to write an entire book to do them justice! Therefore, it is essential to narrow the topic to one that is suitable for a short essay. 
For example, if one of the topics asks you to write about the benefits of a  sport, choose a particular sport in which you are interested. Then, ask questions: What are the benefits? Do they relate to health? If so, is it physical or mental health benefits that you are most interested in?

Follow these steps to narrow the topic you chose in LA 6.
k. Referring to the section “Idea Mapping” in Chapter 4 of Read, Think, Write, create an idea map to help you narrow the topic. Write your general topic in the centre of the map and spend at least five minutes creating a map and gradually coming up with more specific subtopics.
l. Now that you have generated some potential sub-topics, consider which of those topics will be most suitable for your essay. Choose a narrowed topic for your essay.
m. Appy “Checklist 10.1: Developing a Good Topic” to your topic. Does your topic meet the criteria for an effective essay topic, in general, or does it require more work?
n. Recommended: If you are not sure if the topic you have chosen is suitable for Assignment 5, email your tutor for feedback.
Identify search terms
Now that you have chosen and narrowed a topic, it is time to identify search terms that will help you find appropriate sources for your essay.
o. Review the short section “Identifying Keywords for a Research Search” in Chapter 20 of Read, Think, Write.
p. Complete “Practice 20.1” to develop search terms for your topics. Do all four steps: A, B, C, and D.
q. Write down a list of three to five search terms that you will begin with. Ideal search terms are broad enough to generate a number of sources, but narrow enough to not create too long a list of sources to work through. For example, if you type in “The benefits of sport for depression,” you get multiple pages of potential titles, but when you change “sport” to “running,” the list becomes more focused and specific.
r. Once you begin searching (in the next step), you may need to go through a process of trial and error. As you conduct searches, keep a notebook handy and record all of the search terms you have tried. Keep refining the list, making the terms broader or narrower, as needed.
Begin to find research sources.
Once you have a list of search terms, it is time for another visit to the AU Library website.
Note: Do not rely on a Google search to locate scholarly articles. Access to most scholarly articles requires a subscription, which the AU Library has paid so that you can access a wide range of periodicals.
Additionally, when you are first learning about a topic, Wikipedia might be an appropriate place to start, but always move on from Wikipedia. As an open-source website that anyone—with or without credentials—can contribute to, it is not sufficiently trustworthy for academic purposes. 
Therefore, do not quote or paraphrase Wikipedia. This is not a source your tutor will want to see on your citation list. Be equally careful of other questionable websites.
s. Begin the search.
Go to AU Library’s Library and Scholarly Resources page. Enter your search terms and begin to browse available sources. Remember to record the search terms you use.
t. Begin to collect potential articles.
As you go down the rabbit hole of searching for articles, it can be easy to lose track of where you are, and you may find yourself trying to get back to an article you saw earlier.
To avoid this problem, as you hunt, keep track of the articles that seem to be most relevant to your topic. While you can do this with pen and paper, the easiest and most efficient way is to save the permalinks of the articles so you can return to them. Learn how to do that here: 
https://athabascau.libanswers.com/faq/201731 If this feature is unavailable, simply save the PDF to a folder on your computer, as we recommended earlier.
Any time you want to look at your articles, open the folder on your desktop where you saved the PDF of the articles. If you only saved permanent links, simply go to the AU library search area and type in the permanent link.
Be discriminating. Your initial search may generate hundreds of articles. Do not simply take the first ones that pop up. Look carefully at the titles. Keep refining your search terms.
u. Another way to find quality sources is to use Google Scholar. Follow these steps: Open Google Scholar in a new tab (https://scholar.google.com/). Set up the Library Links for AU to access the articles you can get through the library subscriptions. Here's how to set up AU Library Links in Google Scholar. Once you have linked to the library and started to search, anything available through the AU library will be indicated on the right-hand side of the page, where you’ll see the words “Athabasca Univ. Library.” Click there. Some of the articles you find will be free to anyone and won’t require you to access them from the library. If you find an article you like that has no link to the AU library, simply click on the title.
v. Once you have searched in the AU library, you will see important limiters on the left-hand side of the page. Click on “Full Text” and "Scholarly (Peer Reviewed) Journals.: It’s also essential to limit the date so you have access to the most current information possible. You can use the slide bar or simply type in the date range you want. We suggest limiting your search to the last five years for most topics, but some topics will require even more currency, so you might want to limit your search to the last two years.
If you are using Google Scholar, the limiters are on the left, and you will only be able to limit by date, but you must do so.
w. Select an initial list of potentially relevant sources.
Once you have a substantial list of articles, it is time to be selective. From your first (long) list, choose approximately ten titles that look like they might be most relevant to your topic. If there are fewer than ten titles available in your folder, you may have to go back to LA 8 and broaden your search term.
Some, or perhaps all, of the articles you have on your list will be preceded by an abstract. Skim each abstract to make a quick initial decision about which articles should stay on your list of potential research sources and which can be eliminated. Remember that not all of the articles need to completely cover your initial ideas, and sometimes the most interesting articles are the ones that appear to contradict your initial ideas. Do not reject them simply because you disagree.
Refer to “Evaluating Research Sources” in Chapter 20 of Read, Think, Write to help you determine which articles are most relevant and useful. Select an initial list of potentially relevant sources.
x. From the list of ten sources you have quickly reviewed, choose five or six articles that look most promising. If you are unable to identify five or six relevant articles, go back and conduct another search.
Note: Did you know that AU Library employs reference librarians whose job it is to help students find research for materials for their assignments? 
Reference libraries are experts in finding research materials on almost any topic. Visit AU Library’s Get Library Support page for more information. Read the articles Now, carefully read each of the five or six articles you have chosen. Be sure to read the complete article, not just the abstract or the description. Use the active reading strategies you learned in Chapter 3 of Read, Think, Write, which you practiced in Unit 2.
Some articles can be very long, and some parts may relate less to your precise topic, but make sure that you get a good sense of the points the article makes.
y. After you read each article, close or move away from the article before you jot down what you determine to be the main points and thesis.
z. You may want to add a note to indicate whether the information in the article will likely be relevant to your essay topic or not. If you have some critical thoughts about the article, you can add those as well.
aa. For the purpose of an annotated bibliography, it is not necessary to include any quotations, but if something in an article strikes you as particularly profound, do quote it, making sure, of course, to properly cite it so that you do not inadvertently present the direct quotation as something of your own.
bb.After you have completed your notes, make sure to write down the complete and comprehensive bibliographical information for the article. Refer to “Table 20.5” (MLA style) or “Table 20.6” (APA style) in Chapter 20 to ensure you have recorded all the required information.
Create an annotated bibliography Based on the notes you took in LA 9, and with Chapter 20 of Read, Think, Write in mind, begin to compile an annotated bibliography that includes five or six sources, at least three of which are articles from peer-reviewed journals.
To find out whether a journal is peer-reviewed or not, follow these steps:
a. Go to AU’s Library and Scholarly Resources page.
b. Click “Journal title search” and then enter the title of the journal.
c. In the search result, choose the appropriate title, and click “Journal Details.”
For example, a search for “Societies” reveals that Societies is indeed a peer-reviewed journal:
Each entry on the annotated bibliography should begin with a properly formatted bibliographic entry.
Below the bibliographic entry, write a short paragraph (approximately 100 words) that includes:
•	a brief summary of the content of the article, including its thesis, paraphrased in your own words
•	an evaluation of the article’s reliability
•	a reflection on the article’s relevance and applicability to your Assignment 5 essay
